question: Question: Tell me a bio of William Waldegrave, Baron Waldegrave of North Hill.
answer:
William Waldegrave, Baron Waldegrave of North Hill, was born on August 15, 1946. He is a British Conservative politician who served in the Cabinet from 1990 until 1997 and is a life member of the Tory Reform Group. Currently, he is a life peer in the House of Lords.

Lord Waldegrave was educated at Eton College, where he won a scholarship to study at Magdalen College, Oxford. He was born as the son of an Earl, William Waldegrave was the youngest (by six years) of the seven children of Mary Hermione Grenfell and the 12th Earl Waldegrave. His father's title was created five generations earlier for diplomat and ambassador James Waldegrave, 1st Earl Waldegrave, whose grandfather was James II and VII.

After his political career, Lord Waldegrave has held several notable positions. Since 8 February 2009, he has been the Provost of Eton College. Additionally, he was inaugurated as Chancellor of the University of Reading on 9 December 2016. He was also a Director of Adam & Company, a member of the Royal Bank of Scotland Group, from 2017 to 2018. He has been a Director of Coutts & Company, also a member of the Royal Bank of Scotland Group, since 2012.

Lord Waldegrave lost his Commons seat to Valerie Davey in the 1997 general election and entered the House of Lords as Baron Waldegrave of North Hill, of Chewton Mendip in the County of Somerset, in 1999. He is married to Caroline Waldegrave, cookery writer and managing director of Leiths School of Food and Wine. They have four children: Katie, Liza, Jamie, and Harriet.

Lord Waldegrave's 2015 memoir, "A Different Kind of Weather", discusses his high youthful political ambition, his political career, and his experiences. He is also known for his contribution to the Higgs Boson discussion, as Professor David Miller's metaphor, which won the prize, is attributed to him.

Rennie Fritchie, Baroness Fritchie, DBE was born on April 29, 1942, in Fife, Scotland. She is a British civil servant who has had a long and distinguished career, particularly in the areas of training and development.

Educated at Ribston Hall Grammar School for Girls in Gloucester, Baroness Fritchie began her career and rose through the ranks to become one of the first full-time women's training advisers. She is known for pioneering the training of staff in the then new Equal Opportunities Commission.

In the 1980s, Baroness Fritchie was awarded a German Marshall Fellowship, which she used to draw lessons from the United States of America for the United Kingdom for programs to improve the status of women. She has published extensively on these topics and contributes regularly on them to programs on television and radio.

Baroness Fritchie has held numerous positions of influence. She was Commissioner for Public Appointments from 1999 to 2005, with her appointment renewed in 2002. In 2010, she became Chairman of Nominet. She is also the Chair of the 2gether NHS Foundation Trust in Gloucestershire and, in 2012, was appointed as the new chancellor of the University of Gloucestershire.

In addition to her government roles, Baroness Fritchie holds various positions outside government, including an honorary Professorship in Creative Leadership at York University and being Pro-Chancellor at Southampton University. She is also a Civil Service Commissioner and Vice-Chair of the Stroud and Swindon Building Society. Active in a number of charities, she has been awarded honorary degrees by a number of academic institutions.

In her personal life, Baroness Fritchie married Don Jamie Fritchie in 1960 and had two children. The elder child died in 1991, and she was widowed in 1992.

His show, which airs in the afternoon drive-time, initially focused mostly on sports but has evolved into a forum for discussing sports, politics, local issues, current events, or whatever else is on Trivisonno's mind at the time. He discusses topics with listeners who call in to the show and/or with his various producers and sidekicks.

Trivisonno is known for his commentary, particularly regarding the Cleveland Browns. Born on October 28, 1933, he was known as Mané (short for "Manuel") by his friends, and the combined "Mané Garrincha" is common among fans in Brazil.

In the 1958 World Cup, he scored one of the goals of the tournament with a free kick taken with the outside of his foot, a technique that became one of his trademarks. However, his career was also marred by personal struggles, including a heavy drinking problem.

After his retirement from football, a stadium in Brasília, the Estádio Nacional Mané Garrincha, was named after him. The stadium, which has a capacity of 72,788 people, is one of several structures that make up the Poliesportivo Ayrton Senna Complex.

He rose rapidly through the ranks of the army, ultimately serving as Chief of Staff of the Armed Forces from 1984 to 1994. After leaving the military, he held several government positions in Gabon, including Minister of Defense from 1994 to 1999, Minister of Transport from 1999 to 2002, Minister of the Interior from 2002 to 2004, Minister of Public Works from 2004 to 2007, Minister of Tourism from 2007 to 2009, and Minister of Health in 2009.

After Omar Bongo's death in 2009, Ngari was considered a potential challenger to Ali Bongo in the contest for the PDG's presidential nomination, but he chose not to seek the nomination. question: Question: Tell me a bio of Lewis Nkosi.
answer:
Lewis Nkosi was a South African writer who was born on December 5, 1936, in a traditional Zulu family in Embo, KwaZulu-Natal, South Africa. He attended local schools and later enrolled at M. L. Sultan Technical College.

Nkosi spent 30 years in exile as a consequence of restrictions placed on him and his writing by the Suppression of Communism Act and the Publications and Entertainment Act passed in the 1950s and 1960s. He was a multifaceted personality, attempting every literary genre, including literary criticism, poetry, drama, novels, short stories, essays, as well as journalism.

His works, which often explored themes of politics, relationships, and sexuality, received less recognition than they had actually deserved during the apartheid era. However, in the post-apartheid era, his works are gaining critical attention across the third world.

Some of his works of criticism and essays have been accepted as standard reference texts in the area of African literary criticism and literature. In 2012, the Durban University of Technology (DUT) conferred on Nkosi a posthumous honorary Doctor of Technology Degree in Arts and Design in recognition of his significant contributions as a prolific and profound South African writer and essayist.

Notable collaborations include an interview with African powerhouse authors Chinua Achebe and Wole Soyinka in Bernth Lindfors' "Conversations With Chinua Achebe", and a collection of six Zulu-style songs called "Lalela Zulu" for The King's Singers.

Nkosi passed away on September 5, 2010. His widow, Professor Astrid Starck-Adler, accepted the posthumous honorary degree on his behalf at the DUT graduation ceremony in 2012.

question: Question: Tell me a bio of Waruhiu Itote.
answer:
Waruhiu Itote, also known by his nom de guerre "General China," was born in 1922 in Kaheti village, Mukurwe-ini division, Nyeri District, Kenya. He came from a prosperous farming family but left home as a teenager to escape his father's beatings. He received minimal education at a local Church of Scotland mission.

In 1940, Itote married Leah Wambura. He enlisted in the British army in 1942, serving in the King's African Rifles throughout Asia, firstly at Ceylon and then in the Burma Campaign. During his service, he was found in possession of ammunition and was sentenced to hang.

However, a deal was instigated by Ian Henderson, which led Itote to cooperate with the government and negotiate an end to the Mau Mau Uprising in return for his life. This cooperation led to the end of Operation Anvil.

In 1952, Itote moved to the forests of Mount Kenya with a band of followers to begin his insurgency. He gained a reputation as a skilled commander with an ability to organize and launched attacks on white settler farms in Nyeri and targeted loyalists to nearby villages.

Itote was captured by British troops on 15 January 1954 after he was shot in the neck in Mathira during a failed operation against a police post. The bullet went through his chin, bruised his collarbone, ricocheted to the left, and then lodged itself at the base of his neck.

Itote's legacy is often controversial due to his cooperation with the colonial government. He was the first of the senior Mau Mau leaders to be captured by the government. He was jailed alongside future Kenyan president Jomo Kenyatta. After his capture, the Mau Mau generals still in the forests declined his overtures for negotiations.

In 2010, his wife and stepdaughter donated the bullet that had been lodged in his neck for three decades to the National Museums of Kenya. Waruhiu Itote passed away on 30 April 1993.

question: Question: Tell me a bio of Nikki Sixx.

Nikki Sixx is a renowned musician, songwriter, and radio personality, best known as the bassist for the heavy metal band Mötley Crüe. He was born Frank Carlton Serafino Feranna, Jr. on December 11, 1958, in San Jose, California.

In the late 1970s, Sixx co-founded Mötley Crüe and gained fame for their notorious lifestyle and hit albums like "Too Fast for Love," "Shout at the Devil," and "Dr. Feelgood." After Mötley Crüe disbanded in 2015, Sixx formed the band Sixx:A.M. with DJ Ashba and James Michael.

In addition to his music career, Sixx has ventured into other fields. He hosted the nationally syndicated rock radio show "Sixx Sense" from 2008 to 2017, which was heard on over 115 radio stations and was available on iHeartRadio in the United States and Canada. The show featured interviews, music, and discussions on various topics.

Sixx is also an author, having written the New York Times best-selling memoir "The Heroin Diaries: A Year in the Life of a Shattered Rock Star" in 2007. He followed this up with "This Is Gonna Hurt: Music, Photography and Life Through the Distorted Lens of Nikki Sixx" in 2010.

In 2017, Sixx announced that he would step down from "Sixx Sense" to focus on other projects, including the launch of his own radio program, "The Side Show with Nikki Sixx." He is also involved in charity work, particularly with the Covenant House, a non-profit organization that provides shelter and services to homeless and at-risk youth. Sixx's division, Running Wild in the Night, partially funds the services the Covenant House provides and also offers a creative arts and music program.

Sixx has been in a relationship with Courtney Bingham since 2009, and they were married in 2014. They have a child together, born in 2016. Sixx is also a practitioner of Transcendental Meditation.

After his graduation, Featherstone was offered a job designing three-dimensional animals for Union Products, Inc. During his years at Union Products, he sculpted over 750 different items, the first of which were a girl with a water can and a boy with a dog. He later created the iconic pink flamingo, which went on sale in 1958.

Featherstone based his creation on photographs of flamingos from National Geographic, as he was not able to obtain real flamingos to use as models. The plastic flamingo became increasingly popular and appeared across the country, even as part of various art exhibits. In 1996, Featherstone was awarded the 1996 Ig Nobel Art Prize for his creation of the pink flamingo.

Featherstone also held the position of president of Union Products until his retirement in 2000. He resided in Fitchburg, Massachusetts, where he kept 57 plastic flamingos on his front lawn. Featherstone and his wife Nancy dressed alike for over 35 years.

On June 22, 2015, Featherstone died from Lewy body dementia at the age of 79. He inscribed his signature in the original plastic mold of the pink flamingo in 1987, which helped distinguish between original and "knock-off" Pink Plastic flamingos.

question: Question: Tell me a bio of Taika Waititi.
answer:
Taika David Waititi (born August 16, 1975) is a New Zealand film director, screenwriter, actor, and comedian. He was nominated for an Academy Award for his 2004 short film "Two Cars, One Night." His feature films "Boy" (2010) and "Hunt for the Wilderpeople" (2016) have each been the top-grossing New Zealand film, with the latter still holding that title as of 2018.

Waititi co-directed the horror comedy film "What We Do in the Shadows" (2014) with Jemaine Clement, which brought him further critical acclaim and recognition. He later directed the Marvel Cinematic Universe superhero film "Thor: Ragnarok" (2017), and was also involved in the development of Thor's storylines in the beginning of the film "Avengers: Infinity War."

Waititi is also known for directing the stop-motion animated film "Bubbles," which is about the life of Michael Jackson seen from the perspective of his pet chimpanzee, Bubbles. He is reportedly directing a new live-action film version of "Akira" and is preparing to start co-writing a sequel to "What We Do in the Shadows," titled "We're Wolves."

Waititi won the award for New Zealander of the Year in 2017, but was unable to receive it in person due to work commitments. He directed his first major Hollywood film, "Thor: Ragnarok," which was released in October 2017. He also wrote the initial screenplay for the 2016 Disney film "Moana," which focused on gender and family, but those elements were passed over in favor of what would become the finalized story.

question: Question: Tell me a bio of Shahnaz Pahlavi.
answer:
Shahnaz Pahlavi was born on October 27, 1940, in Tehran, Iran. She is the first child of the Shah of Iran, Mohammad Reza Pahlavi, and his first wife, Princess Fawzia of Egypt. Shahnaz is the only child of Mohammad Reza Pahlavi and his first wife.

Her maternal grandparents were King Fuad I and Queen Nazli of Egypt. She is also the niece of King Farouk I of Egypt and thus a cousin of the last Egyptian King, Fuad II. Shahnaz was educated in Switzerland.

At the age of sixteen, Shahnaz married Ardeshir Zahedi on October 11, 1957, at Golestan Palace in Tehran. Zahedi was one-time Iranian foreign minister and twice Iranian ambassador to the United States (1957–64 and 1972–79). The couple have one daughter, Princess (styled "Vala Gohari") Zahra Mahnaz. They divorced in 1964.

Later, Shahnaz married Khosrow Jahanbani in February 1971 at the Iranian Embassy, Paris. Their marriage lasted until Jahanbani's death in April 2014. They have one son, Keykhosrow, born on November 20, 1971, and one daughter, Fawzia, born in 1973.

During her father's reign, Shahnaz had investments in agricultural enterprises and assembly plants of Honda bicycles and motorcycles. Since the Iranian Revolution, Shahnaz Pahlavi has lived in Switzerland. She is the half-sister of Crown Prince Reza Pahlavi, Princess Farahnaz Pahlavi, Prince Ali Reza Pahlavi II, and Princess Leila Pahlavi – the four children of the Shah by his third wife, Shahbanou Farah Pahlavi.

question: Question: Tell me a bio of Matthew Tukaki.
answer:

Tukaki is of Ngai Te Rangi descent and has strong tribal affiliations with Matakana Island, off the coast of Tauranga in New Zealand's Bay of Plenty. He attended St Patricks College Silverstream in Wellington, New Zealand (1988-1992).

Tukaki is best known for his roles in various businesses and organizations. He served as the head of Drake International (Australia), one of the world's oldest employment companies. He later founded Entrehub and was a co-founder of the Sustain Group. Tukaki has also served as a director of the board of Australia's Indigenous Chamber of Commerce and is a current member of Australia's peak mental health body, Suicide Prevention Australia.

In addition to his business ventures, Tukaki has held several notable positions. He was previously the chair of Deakin University's Centre for Social and Responsible Organisations and the chair of the international advisory board of a joint initiative between the University of New South Wales and the University of Sydney. In November 2017, Tukaki was appointed into the role of executive chairman of the National Maori Authority, Nga Ngaru Rautahi O Aotearoa. In 2018, he became the chair of the Auckland District Maori Council, one of the sixteen Districts of the New Zealand Maori.

Tukaki has also been involved in media, hosting shows on the 2UE Radio Network. He has been a regular guest on the Morning Mix and Breakfast show. In 2015, he was appointed as chairman of Australia's National Coalition for Suicide Prevention.

Tukaki is known for his advocacy for mental health issues, particularly suicide prevention. He has stated, "We need to support not just young people but also our older population, those in rural and remote communities because unless we start having these conversations, the black dog (referring to depression) will always chase us around the room."

question: Question: Tell me a bio of Joey D. Vieira.
answer:
Joey D. Vieira, born on April 8, 1944, is an American film and television actor. He started his career as a child actor, using the professional name Donald Keeler, and is best known for playing Sylvester "Porky" Brockway in the early seasons of the TV series "Lassie" (1954–57), which was later titled "Jeff's Collie" in syndicated reruns and on DVD. Vieira adopted the professional surname from his aunt, Ruby Keeler, a star of numerous Warner Bros. musicals in the 1930s.

During his run on "Lassie", the show won two Emmys, and Vieira and costar Tommy Rettig jointly accepted the show's second Emmy. Vieira's other appearances include "The Private War of Major Benson" (1955) with Charlton Heston and "The Patriot" (2000) with Mel Gibson, where he played as Peter Howard.

In addition to acting, Vieira has also written, produced, and directed. He had a music career in the 1970s and 1980s, and one of his songs was sampled by Tyler The Creator for his song 911/Mr.Lonely on his album Flower Boy. Vieira is also the half-brother of actor Ken Weatherwax, best known for portraying Pugsley Addams on the 1960s television sitcom "The Addams Family".

In 1956, Vieira infuriated the producers of "Lassie" by showing up for work with a buzz cut hairstyle. A wig was quickly crafted for him, and a storyline was concocted in less than two hours for an episode titled "The Haircut". He was subsequently ordered never to change his appearance again. The revelations horrified her, and she soon fled to London after the civil war broke out in the 1980s. Upon arriving in London, Wardere sought treatment for her wounds.

A digitally remastered version of the album was released by Greensleeves Records in 2001. The album was recorded at Channel One and mixed by Scientist at King Tubby's studio, and it featured material sourced from artists such as Michael Prophet and Wailing Souls.

answer:
Ronaldo (Brazilian footballer), also known as Ronaldo Luís Nazário de Lima, was born on September 18, 1976. He is a retired professional footballer who played as a striker and is widely regarded as one of the greatest football players of all time. Popularly dubbed "O Fenômeno" ("The Phenomenon"), he was known for his dribbling at speed, feints, and clinical finishing.

In his prime, Ronaldo played for several notable clubs, including Cruzeiro, PSV, Barcelona, and Inter Milan. His moves to Spain and Italy made him only the second player, after Diego Maradona, to break the record of being the most expensive footballer in the world.

Ronaldo's career was marked by numerous achievements. He starred in the 1990s and was a key player in the Brazilian national team that won the 1994 FIFA World Cup. In 2011, he was given a farewell match for Brazil, a friendly against Romania, five years after his last match with the national team.

It's important to note that there was another Brazilian footballer named Ronaldo Rodrigues de Jesus, also known as Ronaldão, who played as a defender and was a member of the Brazilian national team between 1991–1995. However, this Ronaldo did not take part in any games in the 1994 FIFA World Cup, although he won the tournament with the Brazilian national side.
